Senses.Explanation: Literally, the ten directions gather in one assembly. The phrase opens an inherited four-line verse: “the ten directions gather in one assembly; each person learns non-doing; this is the buddha-selection ground; with the mind empty, one passes and returns” (十方同聚會，箇箇學無為；此是選佛場，心空及第歸). Huitang Zuxin quotes the verse as an ancient saying and continues its examination language. Tian'an Sheng speaks the complete verse during an evening assembly. In Yunwai Xingze's record, an unnamed monk turns its first two lines into a question, and Yunwai answers. The retained lamp witness preserves Yuanwu Keqin's expanded variant, which changes the second line to “the original body is not obscured” (本來身不昧) and adds paired lines before naming Layman Pang Yun.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes the Ten Oxen in these Chan records. Its wording is "ten oxen." As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and its associated pictures. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). The sequence begins with named sections including "seeking the ox" (尋牛) and "seeing the tracks" (見跡). The corpus also records direct criticism of its later handling: Baichi calls Liangshan's verses "compassionate, talk that descends into the weeds" (慈悲之故，落草之談), says later people "made a wrong move and then painted these Ten-Ox forms" (錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子), and urges burning them. In an encounter, the identified teacher interrupts the recorded questioner asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?" (牛在甚麼處). The deviation from an ordinary count of cattle is documentary: "the Ten Oxen" (十牛) functions as the proper name of a Chan verse-and-picture series, circulated, recited, questioned, and criticized inside the record.

Senses.Explanation: This deictic expression points back to a just-demonstrated action, wording, interpretation, or state: “in this way,” “like this,” or simply “so.” Huineng asks what is coming “in this way”; Shitou Xiqian blocks “this way,” “not this way,” and both together; Yuanwu Keqin warns that understanding in this way misses the matter, but elsewhere says that seeing in this way gives a share of freedom. The phrase also forms recurrent frames: “at precisely such a time” (正當恁麼時), “if so” (恁麼則), “must be this way” (直須恁麼), and Yuanwu Keqin’s self-reference to “talking this way” (恁麼說話). Foyan Qingyuan juxtaposes repeated “this way” with repeated “not this way,” while Sixin Wuxin says a great man is not made this way. Its translation therefore follows the demonstrative relation in each turn; the word does not itself name a teaching or a single approved manner.

Senses.Explanation: 恁麼道 points to an utterance by the manner in which it is said: to say it this way. Senses.Explanation: All at once is an adverb in narrative accounts of a change after an encounter, answer, or sight. The Five Houses lineage account says that Bajiao Che was all at once greatly awakened after a hall address. The Yune record uses it in the story of seeing the morning star, and the Raising Old Cases compilation says that Yu Di was all at once aware after Yaoshan called him. A lamp case likewise narrates Zifang's all-at-once understanding after Fayan Wenyi's replies. In these retained passages, the narrator reports the change; the word is not itself an answer or the name of a separate condition.
